CausalChain: Catechins chelate transition metals (Fe, Cu) -> Reduction in metal-catalyzed antioxidant defense -> Increase in intracellular oxidative stress -> Inhibition of IL-8 signaling -> Decrease in angiogenesis and metastatic support -> Cancer stem cell niche becomes inhospitable -> Induction of apoptosis and impaired self-renewal in cancer stem cells
Hypothesis: Green tea catechins, through their metal chelating and IL-8 inhibitory activities, create a hostile microenvironment that selectively targets cancer stem cells by elevating oxidative stress and disrupting pro-survival signaling, thereby reducing tumor recurrence and metastasis.
Abstract: Green tea catechins have established roles in cancer prevention and cellular homeostasis through their antioxidant, pro-oxidant, and signaling modulatory activities. Here, we propose that the dual properties of catechins—namely, their capacity to chelate transition metals and inhibit pro-angiogenic IL-8 signaling—create a metal-depleted and oxidative-stress–prone microenvironment that selectively targets cancer stem cells. This altered niche may impair the metabolic and epigenetic programming of these cells, reducing tumorigenicity and metastasis. Our hypothesis provides a novel framework for understanding the selective anticancer effects of green tea catechins and suggests new strategies for adjunctive cancer therapies.
